items.title: Fireworks colours are atomic fingerprints
items.claim: Lithium gives a crimson flame, sodium orange, potassium lilac, copper blue-green, strontium red, barium green. Each element gives a characteristic colour because its electrons fall through fixed energy gaps that are unique to that element.

options.text: Heat excites electrons; they fall back to lower energy levels, emitting photons of specific wavelengths set by the spacing of that element's allowed electron energy levels
The shape of the metal sample
The oxygen content of the flame

items.reveal_title: Spectra are unique signatures of atoms
items.reveal:
Each element has its own set of allowed electron energy levels — fixed by the quantum mechanics of its electrons and nucleus. A flame thermally excites electrons; as they relax, photons emerge with energies exactly equal to the gap between levels (E = hf).

Sodium's strong 'D line' at 589 nm is the 3p-to-3s transition. The bright yellow streetlights in old high-pressure sodium lamps use the same transition.

This is how astronomers identify elements in stars they can never visit: fit dark or bright lines in stellar spectra to known atomic transition wavelengths. Helium was discovered in the Sun (1868, by Janssen and Lockyer) before being isolated on Earth (1895, by Ramsay).
items.why: Flame colours look like a party trick. They are direct measurements of quantum-mechanical energy levels.

items.title: Pure water dissolves more silver chloride than salt water does
items.claim: Silver chloride is famously insoluble — Ksp is about 1.8 times 10 to the minus 10. But it dissolves slightly. Try to dissolve it in salt water and the solubility plummets to almost zero.
items.prompt: Why does adding more Cl- decrease AgCl solubility?

options.text: Le Chatelier — adding more Cl- shifts AgCl(s) is in equilibrium with Ag+ + Cl- back to the left, reducing dissolved Ag+ until [Ag+][Cl-] equals Ksp again
Silver chloride decomposes in salt water
Salt water becomes saturated with itself, leaving no room for AgCl

items.reveal:
Suppose in pure water solubility 's' equals square root of Ksp, around 1.3 times 10 to the minus 5 M for AgCl.

In 0.1 M NaCl, [Cl-] is dominated by the salt (about 0.1 M). [Ag+] must satisfy [Ag+] times 0.1 equals 1.8 times 10 to the minus 10, so [Ag+] is about 1.8 times 10 to the minus 9 M. Solubility drops by a factor of nearly 10,000.

This is exploited in gravimetric analysis: precipitate the analyte by adding excess of a common ion, ensuring almost everything comes out of solution.
items.why: Students think 'dissolved + dissolved = more dissolved'. Le Chatelier flips the intuition for ionic equilibria.

items.title: A reaction that gets cold all by itself
items.claim: Mix solid barium hydroxide octahydrate with solid ammonium thiocyanate in a beaker. The mixture turns into a slush and drops to about minus 20 degrees Celsius — cold enough to freeze the beaker to a wet wooden block.
items.prompt: How can a reaction proceed if it absorbs heat from its surroundings?

options.text: It can't — the textbook is wrong
Endothermic reactions only happen when energy is supplied externally
The enormous increase in entropy (two solids becoming liquid and gas) outweighs the unfavourable enthalpy change in the Gibbs equation
The reaction is actually exothermic at the molecular level — the cooling is an illusion

items.reveal_title: Entropy can drive a reaction uphill in enthalpy
items.reveal:
Gibbs free energy: delta G equals delta H minus T delta S. The reaction is strongly endothermic (positive delta H), but it produces 10 moles of liquid water plus 2 moles of ammonia gas from 2 moles of crystalline solid. The entropy change is huge and positive.

At room temperature T delta S is larger than delta H, so delta G is negative — the reaction is spontaneous and proceeds, sucking heat from the surroundings as it does.
items.why: Students learn 'exothermic equals spontaneous' as a rule of thumb. Entropy can outvote enthalpy when disorder rises sharply.
